projects.title: GlassBox
projects.description: Built a multi-agent lending system where every decision is auditable and every denial comes with a way to fix it, addressing a real gap under ECOA/Reg B, which requires lenders to give specific reasons for a denial rather than a black-box score.7 AI agents (Jac walkers over a provenance graph) assess an application in parallel, then draft a decision. A dedicated No-Discrimination agent reaches its OWN verdict from permissible facts BEFORE seeing the draft, then checks it for reliance on a protected characteristic or a proxy (e.g. ZIP code standing in for race), and can veto in either direction.Key decision: access to protected data is enforced structurally, by graph edge type, not by a prompt — analysts are physically unable to read it, not just asked not to.On a denial, a recourse agent tells the user exactly what to fix, and a Re-check button re-runs the real decision on corrected numbers, so they see a result, not a promise.Stack: Jac for the decision engine, Groq (byLLM) for document reading, Next.js/React frontend. Verdict logic stays fully deterministic.

projects.title: ExoPlanet Hunters
projects.description: Planet Hunters is a machine learning project that uses a convolutional neural network (CNN) to help identify possible exoplanets from astronomical light curve data. The goal is to build an assistant that can analyze patterns in star brightness over time and flag signals that may indicate a planet passing in front of its host star.This project combines astronomy, data science, and deep learning. I wanted to explore how artificial intelligence can support real space exploration by helping scientists search through large amounts of telescope data more efficiently.

projects.title: VibeGuard: AI-Powered Sensory Scanner for Inclusive Spaces
projects.description: Hackathon Project (Arduino + OpenCV + Gemini AI) | Nov 2025Built after noticing neurodivergent classmates hesitate outside loud rooms because of sensory overload. VibeGuard reads a room’s “vibe” and gives a simple report so someone can decide whether to walk in.•Hardware: Elegoo UNO R3 with a microphone, PIR motion sensor, and webcam to capture noise, movement, and activity in real time.•Software: a web app using OpenCV and Google Gemini to turn that data into plain mood labels (Calm, Social, Loud, Overwhelming) with confidence scores and coping tips.•Output: scan a space from a laptop or phone, get an instant report plus a QR-log export.

publications.title: Terrain Aided Navigation for Autonomous Underwater Vehicles with Local Gaussian Processes
publications.description: Navigation of autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) in the subsea environment is particularly challenging due to the unavailability of GPS because of the rapid attenuation of electromagnetic waves in water. As a result, the AUV requires alternative methods for position estimation. This thesis describes a terrain-aided navigation approach for an AUV where, with the help of a prior depth map, the AUV localizes itself using altitude measurements from a multibeam DVL. The AUV simultaneously builds a probabilistic depth map of the seafloor as it moves to unmapped locations. The main contribution of this thesis is a new, scalable, and on-line terrain-aided navigation solution for AUVs which does not require the assistance of a support surface vessel. Simulation results on synthetic data and experimental results from AUV field trials in Panama City, Florida are also presented.

My best friend got married last week. And it hit me harder than I expected. I met Arhum in college. We did everything together back then. Classes, food runs, late nights, all of it. Be the guy that calls for no reason. Be the guy that books the flight. Be the guy that keeps showing up. And do not wait until you are less busy. You will NEVER be less busy. Congrats Arhum. patents.title: Dynamic machine learning hyperparameter tuning for feedback-driven optimization
patents.description: Published with UC San Diego. Traditional machine learning training is a static process that lacks real-time adaptability of hyperparameters. Popular tuning solutions during runtime involve checkpoints and schedulers. Adjusting hyper-parameters usually require the program to be restarted, wasting utilization and time, while placing unnecessary strain on memory and processors. We present LiveTune, a new framework allowing real-time parameter tuning during training through LiveVariables. LiveVariables allow for a continuous training session by storing parameters on designated ports on the system, allowing them to be dynamically adjusted. Extensive evaluations of our framework show saving up to 60 seconds and 5.4 Kilojoules of energy per hyperparameter change.

Everyone's worried about moving too slowly with AI. Almost nobody worries about moving too fast until Legal gets involved. A team rolls out a new AI tool, and there’s an instant spike in productivity, which everyone is happy about. A few months later, security discovers customer data has been processed on infrastructure nobody approved. And now, all of a sudden, your success story becomes an audit process. Speed is key. But speed without governance means technical debt that will inevitably need to be repaid down the road. That's why we built gammaNext differently. It runs natively inside Salesforce, keeps the model in your own Azure environment, and logs every action with permission controls. You get the benefits of AI without losing visibility or control over your data. How is your team balancing AI adoption with governance? I'd be interested to hear what's worked and what hasn't.

Hi, my name is Gary, an incoming sophomore at Berkeley with a very normal resume. To stand out, I asked AI to build my personal portfolio. It took 30 seconds. The portfolio was good. AI-generated personal websites classified as “slop” and “unimpressive” today would’ve been impressive just three years prior. Y Combinator 's motto is "make something people want." I grew up watching two people do exactly that. 32 years ago, my mom started a business from a tiny basement in India with no funding or family backing. She believed in herself and set a goal to design and stitch clothes that people wanted. My dad was just a friend at the time. He helped out while waiting for his U.S. master's visa. When the opportunity finally came, he made the biggest decision of his life and turned it down because he believed in her. They built the business together. Somewhere along the way, they fell in love and got married. Three decades later, they still run it. Their success came from caring deeply. They remembered the small details, went above and beyond for every customer, and treated employees like family. Some of those customers and employees have been with them for more than 20 years. Over the years, they served more than 100,000 people without spending a dollar on marketing. All word of mouth. Their customers became their community and that community became their growth engine. What I learned from them is simple: - Do the unscalable things to build trust and relationships. - Conviction comes before evidence. - Show up every single day. Through every high and low, I never felt the weight of the business at home. Only now do I understand how deliberate that was. The journey always mattered more to them than the milestones. No matter how ambitious or delusional my ideas sounded, I was never told to play it safe. They believed in me unconditionally. Looking back, it was probably inevitable that I would start something of my own. I grew up curious about the physical world. Scout camps, books, questions like why one crop grows only in a dry season or why the same storm floods one town and not the next. That curiosity is a big part of why we are building Mireye (YC S26) . AI agents are starting to act in the real world, but they can't reliably understand it. Ask a model a specific question about a specific place and it guesses. We’re building the infrastructure to change that. Our mission is to index every inch of the earth and make it as queryable as the web. For three decades, my parents built something people wanted. Now it is our turn.

Every AI wave was bottlenecked by data, then unlocked by tooling. CV had ImageNet, then Roboflow. LLMs had the internet, then RLHF. Physical AI has neither. Robot foundation models don't learn from flat images, they learn from trajectories. Synchronized video, depth, proprioception, force, language, action, all time-aligned, all embodiment-specific. Every lab that wants to train one ends up building its own teleop rig, its own storage format, its own QA pipeline from scratch. There's no ImageNet moment yet. No Roboflow moment either. That's starting to change. Formats like RLDS and Hugging Face's LeRobot are becoming the shared language, the LeRobot dataset hub went from about 1,145 datasets to over 58,000 in about a year. Open X-Embodiment is doing for manipulation data what ImageNet did for vision. The demand is showing up everywhere too. Search interest in "physical AI" is up 3.5x year over year. The pattern is the same every time. The models get good before the data infrastructure catches up. Whoever builds the layer that makes the data usable, not just another dataset host, but real tooling for ingest, annotation, and augmentation, ends up owning a foundational piece of the next decade of AI. That's what we're building at phydata. https://phydata.tech/ #PhysicalAI #AIData #RealWorldData #ArtificialIntelligence #Phydata

Four American hard tech companies raised $3.68 billion inside four days. JPMorganChase took part in three of them. What the capital is funding: Hadrian - $1.37B Series D at a $7.87B valuation, running automated factories that make parts for missiles, submarines, and spacecraft. Base Power Company - $1B Series D at $13B post-money, up from $4B ten months earlier, installing home batteries that feed the grid back. Valar Atomics - $1B Series B led by Sequoia at a reported $6B, after its reactor powered an Nvidia Blackwell chip. Mariana Minerals - $310M Series B led by Khosla Ventures at $1.5B, running a Utah copper mine and a Texas lithium project on its own software. JPMorganChase's Strategic Investment Group anchored Hadrian's round, co-led Base Power's, and the bank sat in Valar's $200 million credit facility. That group operates inside a $1.5 trillion, ten-year program built around defense, energy, critical minerals, and frontier technology. Venture firms priced software while banks financed the physical economy. Both are now writing into the same round at the same company, and that combination is what makes a factory or a reactor financeable at venture speed.

I've been pretty quiet about this while we've been building. But we reported Q2 today, and Brian said on the call that AI is the best thing to ever happen to Airbnb, so it feels like the right moment to share what that's looked like. When we built grocery delivery last year, it took about nine months. Airport pickups, launched recently, took six weeks. Same quality bar. That's now the pattern across the company: concept-to-launch time down as much as 60% on key initiatives, and nearly 80% more features and improvements shipped in the first half than the same period last year. One decision I'd highlight: we never measured AI adoption by usage. Plenty of companies spent this year mandating AI and counting tokens. We measured throughput, what ships and whether it's good. Usage took care of itself. We’re just getting started. There’s a lot more coming across search, discovery, recommendations, support and the host experience as we push AI deeper into the product. And we continue to aggressively shift our momentum towards small teams, moving fast, with agents that can carry entire workflows. The goal is simple: make Airbnb feel more intuitive, more personalized and easier to use for our community. I'm really proud of the team. A shift like this doesn't come from a model release, mandate or a new tool (or even a new CTO). It comes from thousands of engineers willing to change how they work, all at once, without lowering the bar. The momentum is real, and the best part is how early we still are. https://lnkd.in/gNzuzSgY

As a business school professor, I’m always urging my students to set clear goals, make a plan, be ambitious, and be intentional. I often remind them: “You can’t get anywhere if you don’t know where you’re going.” Well....sometimes life has other plans. Exactly three months ago, a freak accident left me with a fractured ankle and five broken metatarsals in my foot. Surgery followed, along with two months in a cast, then a boot, unable to walk. Suddenly, things I had always taken for granted - walking, climbing stairs, showering, driving, traveling - became impossible. I became dependent on others in a way I had never experienced before, and those first two months were incredibly difficult. It was a stark reminder that, despite our best intentions, life doesn’t always go according to plan. We can set goals and chart a course, but we also have to learn to adapt, accept what we cannot control, and appreciate what we often take for granted. Fortunately, I can now walk without a cane - and it feels wonderful! Looking forward to the start of the semester in less than two weeks - I’ll keep telling my students to have a destination in mind, but perhaps with one addition: be prepared for life to change the route. A Big Thank You to my family and friends for their kindness and support. Special shout out to Tara , Shanker and Nikhil !

projects.title: Ozera
projects.description: A full-stack platform designed for LLM researchers with a focus on interpretability that lets users experiment on and visualize the internal mechanics of large language models as they generate text. It provides two from-scratch transformer LLMs alongside many open-source models, with tools for activation patching, attention head analysis, sparse autoencoder experimentation, custom model training, and publication-ready figure exports.Key Features:• Real-time layer-by-layer activation, attention, embeddings, and logit visualization during inference• Activation intervention & patching playground to test causal hypotheses about model behavior• Automated attention head classification (induction, copying, positional, sink) and pattern mining• Sparse autoencoder analysis, feature browsing, and cross-model feature comparison• Custom model training pipeline with dataset upload, cost estimation, and GPU job tracking• Credit-based access to compute for model training, inference, and experiments• Publication-ready figure export with NeurIPS, ICLR, and ICML formatting presetsTechnical Implementation:• Models: Two transformer-based LLMs and corresponding sparse autoencoders built from scratch (no ML frameworks, just math)• Frontend: React 18 / TypeScript with D3, Plotly, Recharts, and Visx for interactive activation and attention visualizations• Backend: FastAPI with Supabase for authentication and PostgreSQL database, plus Stripe for credit-based billing• Compute: Serverless GPU inference on Modal using PyTorch and HuggingFace Transformers, with forward hooks• Deployment: Vercel for frontend, Railway for backendLive at: ozera.app

projects.description: Jamify is an AI-powered web application that curates personalized Spotify playlists based on user-provided descriptions. Leveraging Python, Flask, the Spotify Web API, and the OpenAI API, the project interprets natural language inputs to search for music recommendations that align with user preferences and moods. The application is deployed on Heroku, ensuring seamless accessibility without the need for complex infrastructure management.Key features of Jamify include:- AI-Powered Playlist Generation: Utilizes the OpenAI API to analyze and interpret user inputs, transforming them into tailored search terms that are fed into the Spotify Web API.- Spotify Web API Integration: Retrieves search terms and track data from user inputs to generate playlists dynamically based on user preferences.- Web-Based Interface: Built with Flask to provide an intuitive and responsive user experience.- Error Handling & Robustness: Implemented thorough error handling mechanisms to manage API failures and edge cases.- Deployment on Heroku: Ensuring smooth and cost-effective deployment without the need for manual infrastructure management.The project was developed using Visual Studio Code IDE, taking advantage of its powerful debugging and development tools. Additionally, Flask-Mail was integrated to facilitate whitelist requests, enabling secure user authentication workflows via email.Check out Jamify here: https://bit.ly/jamifyNote: Due to limitations in Spotify Web API's development mode, access to the playlist generation is limited to users on a whitelist. However, getting on the whitelist is simple. Open Jamify in your browser, log in through Spotify, attempt to generate a playlist, and then enter your Spotify email to be added to the whitelist.

projects.title: LungSense.AI
projects.description: LungSense.AI is a specialized web application that leverages artificial intelligence to provide users with a clear, data-driven confidence score indicating their potential risk of lung cancer. By answering a brief yet intuitive questionnaire, users receive a personalized analysis based on health and environmental factors associated with lung cancer risk.The development involved significant technical and research-driven efforts. I started by creating a custom dataset tailored specifically for the model's training and testing needs. Instead of relying on publicly available datasets on Kaggle, which often lacked meaningful correlations between features and outcomes, I developed a rule-based dataset generation algorithm. This algorithm incorporated weighted features, biases, and mathematical relationships grounded in extensive research on the key contributors to lung cancer risk.The model development process was rigorous, as I had several machine learning algorithms trained, fine tuned, and validated through cross validation, grid search, and gradient-based optimization techniques. Ultimately, a Logistic Regression model was selected as the final model due to its superior performance in accuracy and reliability.I implemented the model into the backend by writing an API in Flask, enabling robust API functionality for processing user inputs and delivering real-time predictions. To maintain simplicity and scalability, no database was used, as user inputs are processed in real-time.I then created a seamless and efficient user experience on the frontend in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Designed for simplicity and accessibility, ensuring users could easily navigate the questionnaire and understand the results. To make the application widely accessible, it was deployed on Heroku, leveraging its scalability and ease of integration. DISCLAIMER: This project does not provide medical diagnosis, and is simply a showcase of machine learning development.

Thrilled to share that our paper has been accepted into ACL SRW 2025! I look forward to presenting our work this week at the #1 ranked NLP conference in the world: ACL 2025 in Vienna, Austria. Our paper investigates whether large language models of different sizes converge on similar internal concepts. Using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and similarity metrics like SVCCA and RSA, we analyzed and quantified feature universality between Google 's Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B models. Our results reveal novel multi-token subspace similarity, validate strong alignment of semantic features in the mid-layers of both models, and provide evidence that LLMs carve the world into broadly similar, interpretable features regardless of scale. We hope these findings move us closer to building cross-model interpretability tools and improving LLM safety and control through a deeper understanding of shared internal representations. A huge thank you to my incredible co-authors: Daniel Son , Sanjana Rathore , Andrew W. As I enter the last week of my internship at LinkedIn , I wanted to look back on what I’ve accomplished and share some of the biggest things I’ve learned along the way. For the past 12 weeks, I’ve been building AI agents that help LinkedIn engineering teams understand and optimize their Microsoft Azure spend, alongside Olaoluwa James-Owolabi , Taeeun Kim , and my manager, Shweta Sahni . 1) Being a good teammate means more than just “doing your tasks.” Working on a team means everyone has their own responsibilities, but I learned pretty quickly that being a good teammate goes beyond just getting your own work done. Sometimes that means slowing down to review someone else’s code, moving faster when someone is waiting on you, communicating when you’re blocked, or putting your own task aside for a little while to help unblock someone else. 2) Working in a large codebase means learning what already exists before building something new. We were contributing to a codebase with over a million lines of code, and one of my biggest takeaways was how important it is to understand how similar problems have already been approached before jumping into your own solution. That meant looking through existing code, speaking with other teams, and making sure what I was building was up to the same quality as the code already in production. 3) AI works best when the problem is clearly defined. AI can write quality code and documentation quickly, but it can also go off track just as fast if the task isn’t clearly defined. I learned to break larger stories into smaller, well-defined tasks and spend more time upfront thinking through the approach and refining the plan before any code was written. Being deliberate about what I wanted to build, questioning assumptions along the way, and using AI to help execute led to better code, cleaner pull requests, and a stronger understanding of everything I was shipping.

Last night we won first place at SpaceXAI ‘s Grokathon 🔥🔥 We wanted to answer the question: If we gave agents all the tools that security professionals use to reverse engineer binaries, can we let grok reverse engineer decade old binaries made for gameboys and others platforms? Turns out we can :) We built a custom harness that allowed grok to reverse engineer binaries via static analysis, memory inspection + debugging, and dynamic computer use interaction. We were able to rewrite old gameboy ROMs up to 262kb in size to standard C, which then allowed us to remix and reimagine games. We posted our app on X and other platforms and received 2500 views and ~130 verified users in 12 hours. We even took this a step further. We found a 1995 BMW’s engine control unit’s (ECU) ROM, performed static analysis on it and built a clean-room implementation that allowed us to analyze the engine control signals during steady state operation. Since no existing emulator can properly simulate the ROM, we used what we learned from static analysis to patch an existing open source emulator, and was able to fully emulate the 1995 ROM initial cranking sequence. Shoutout to my awesome teammates Theo Chapman and Supratik Panuganti . Yall are the goats 🐐 #hackathon #grokathon

I spent this past week at GE Vernova's ENERGY2LEAD conference in Greenville, SC. Roughly a quarter of the world's electricity is generated on GE Vernova technology, and you feel that standing next to a machine that weighs half a million pounds and is still built to tolerances finer than a human hair. Reading that is one thing. Standing next to it is another. What surprised me most was how much of the week was built around us rather than around the company. Communication workshops, a business challenge, and a lot of unstructured time with engineers who were honest about their own paths. I came in expecting to learn about turbines. I left understanding myself better, and with a much clearer picture of what I want the next few years to look like. The other thing that stuck: the Edison Engineering Development Program. The Edison Engineers who came to talk with us were the most enthusiastic people in the building. That said more about how GE Vernova treats development than any slide could, and one of them explained how the program let her pursue a master's alongside industry work, which reframed a decision I'd been going back and forth on for a while. Greenville was a nice surprise too. The site isn't an office park in the middle of nowhere. It's a real city with a walkable downtown, beautiful greenery, and a waterfall in the middle of it. This one hurts. Pretty dark day for Nepal. Rest in peace, Nimsdai. Nirmal Purja came from just a small village in the Dhaulagiri foothills, but eventually gained global recognition for his crazy mountaineering efforts. He starred in the Netflix documentary "14 Peaks", but what he should be most known for is something simpler but way more profound, giving Nepali people hope and optimism. People coming from small countries understand this deeply. We don't have many role models in the big "world stage." We cheer everyone of our own. We're still not that far removed from the agricultural subsistence farming lifestyle of our parents/grandparents, so seeing someone succeed and inspire people on the global stage is very rare. Nimsdai is 1 of 1 in this regard. There are very few people bringing an entire country together, and it is devastating to see his light extinguished. I am inspired everyday to work as hard as I do, to have some sort of similar impact in the world stage. Here's to you, Nimsdai. We all have to climb our own mountains, you've shown us how to do so!

publications.title: Machine-learning Prediction of Type-III Instabilities and Spontaneous Energy Localization
publications.subtitle: Journal of Applied Nonlinear Dynamics
publications.description: Modulational instability of a plane-wave mode is known to lead to spontaneous energy localization in nonlinear lattices without the presence of impurities. Where the energy dynamically localizes in the system is highly sensitive to initial conditions. Here we numerically investigate sine-Gordon-type lattices and first show that spatial smoothing of the observed dynamical variables on the lattice can already substantially improve predictions of the eventual localization site from early-time data traces alone, suggesting that the type-III instability that forms the energy hotspot is sensitive to energetic clusters. We then show that machine learning leads to additional dramatic improvement in prediction accuracy. Finally, we also examine the role of chain impurities in determining the localization site.

I don’t think anyone is ever fully qualified when they take on a new project. Regardless of what they’re doing. Alan Yu and I certainly weren’t when we decided to build a robot in our dorm last semester. We were: - first-year engineering students - with little to no design or CAD experience - who had never touched an embedded system - and probably shouldn’t be trusted with electronics in general So why on earth did we want to build a six-legged robot? I could tell you about how I think hardware modularity is the future. I could pitch you on how designs are moving away from big, rigid structures to flexible, plug-and-play components that can be swapped, upgraded or repurposed on the fly. I could walk you through how a modular architecture dramatically shortens iteration cycles, with each component as an independent unit you can test, break, and rebuild without touching the rest. I could even explain to you how that same modularity means swapping out an end effector for a different task—a gripper, a sensor, a drill—takes minutes, not a full redesign. But really, we just thought it would be fun. V1 @ Michigan ’s Product Studio—an incubator where builders take ideas from ‘maybe’ to working product—encouraged us to run with it. We felt that we’d learn a lot from building it, even if it didn’t work. But it worked. Well, sort of. After a few weeks of hard work, we had a moving, modular hexapod robot. As you can imagine, a dorm room isn’t exactly a robotics factory, and our setup was far from perfect. But seeing it actually move… that made every late night, every soldering burn worth it. So next time you have some wild new idea and an itch to build it—you should probably just say yes ;) *pictured below: the bot taking its first steps.*

Why create robot intelligence for just one hand, when we could have it learn from many? GEN-1, our latest embodied foundation model, now supports a broad range of end effectors from 5-finger hands, to specialized tools, and everything in between. Each hand is a different sensorimotor interface by which GEN-1 experiences the physical world. Scaling pretraining across thousands of these interfaces teaches GEN-1 a universal physical commonsense that transfers to new hands and new ways to grasp, push, pull, twist, and more. Nature didn’t converge on just a single solution for manipulating the physical world. It exploded into millions. You can see this everywhere in the diversity of life around us: from the beak of a bird, to the trunk of an elephant, from the suction pads of an octopus, to the pollen baskets of a honeybee. The human hand is only a single point in a design space so large we’ve barely begun to map. For machines, five-fingered hands will just be one tool among many; limiting robots to only that would be a failure of imagination. If we can build general intelligence that understands the underlying physics of interaction, then the shape of the hand becomes secondary to the intelligence that drives it. A suction pad, a gripper, a brush, a plasma welding nozzle – are all just different interfaces through which the same intelligence can reshape the physical world. The future of robot hands won’t look like ours. It will look more like a toolbox with a thousand hands: augmented, recombined, and scaled. Robots were always meant to extend what humans can do – to empower people to shape the physical world in places and at scales we never could before. "The recruiters who win are the ones who actually listen when it matters." I wrote that a year ago. But I should be clear what I mean by winning. It's not by closing this candidate. It's about the person you chose to be every time you have a conversation. Hiring is fundamentally a market. One where if you're not hiring the best, someone else is. So yes, it's competitive. But competitive doesn't mean we get to forget how to treat people through what's already a brutal process. Here's the part AI hasn't changed: what actually earns a candidate's respect looks the same as it always did. A fair conversation. Paying attention. Incumbents can't win on the product anymore, so they compete on the rulebook instead. I've watched this happen in industry after industry, and it's happening again right now. Taxi companies couldn't out-compete Uber on price or convenience. So in 2016, Austin's taxi industry got the city to require fingerprint background checks for ride-share drivers, on top of the checks Uber and Lyft already ran. Voters subsequently voted yes on it at the ballot box causing Uber and Lyft to leave the city rather than comply. Hotel chains ran the same play against Airbnb in New York, outspending them on political contributions more than 30 to 1. Local Law 18 passed in 2022, requiring hosts to register and be physically present for any stay under 30 days. It functionally ended most short-term listings in the city. Hotel rates rose within eighteen months. Hotel revenue rose with them, by an estimated $2 billion or more. Neither industry proved the newer competitor was unsafe. They just made it expensive or illegal enough to stop being viable. David Sacks made a similar case this week about a very different industry. He's argued Anthropic and OpenAI are pushing states to adopt tougher AI rules one after another, each stricter law giving the next state cover to go further, weaponizing regulatory uncertainty to lock out open-weight models like China's Kimi K3. Anthropic's own leadership has floated something like an FAA for AI. Sacks' answer: an approval process built for aircraft, on an aircraft's timeline, would be fatal to a technology that ships new versions every few months. Whether or not that's the intent, the mechanism is identical to what taxis and hotels already ran. You don't need to win on the merits if you can make winning on the merits illegal first. Where do you see this playing out before anyone's willing to call it by name? ...more

Just won Most Technical Hack at University of California, Berkeley 's AI Hackathon! We built a tool that has the potential to accelerate cancer drug discovery: a multi-agent system that takes a tumor mutation profile and tells you which drugs might actually work, and why. -> Workbench: upload a LUAD mutation CSV, and a knowledge graph + LLM pipeline maps your mutations onto activated pathways, identifies coverage gaps, and routes to targeted therapies. Where the graph has no direct answer (which happens more than you'd think), an ML classifier trained on DepMap LUAD data predicts pathway vulnerabilities. It flags the gap, makes a call, and labels it as ML-predicted, so a clinician or researcher knows exactly what to trust. The system doesn't just return drugs. It generates a mechanistic report citing the exact subgraph it traversed, since clinical AI that can’t show its work isn’t useful to researchers in the field. It was invaluable to get real-time 1:1 technical feedback from Fetch.ai , Redis , and Annapurna Labs , and the chance to demo to Anthropic 's team in person. Huge thanks to my amazing teammates Charity G. , Shruti Shah , and Shivnarain Sarin for shipping something real under serious time pressure, and thanks to the Cal Hacks team for the well-run event!

In many ways, the work of a student is easy. We risk very little, yet enjoy a position over those who offer up their knowledge and their selves to our judgment. We enter the classroom carelessly, expecting our professors to serve us the fruits of their lifelong labor. But the bitter truth we students must face is that, in the grand scheme of things, these titans of the corporate world are sacrificing their most precious gift for us: their time. Having weathered the trials of extraordinary careers, rather than devoting well-deserved rest to family, loved ones, and personal pursuits, they choose to stand before us to illuminate our minds. Minds that, all too often, fail to grasp the sheer depth and beauty of the canvas being painted right before our eyes. In my final quarter, I experienced something extraordinary: a revelation that rocked me to my core, evoking that quiet reverence that stills the chest before the "Mona Lisa" or beneath the vaults of the "Sistine Chapel". That experience was the MGMT 550: CEO And Board Governance class at the Foster School of Business, taught by true virtuosos of their craft: Jeff R. (President and CEO at Premera Blue Cross) and Connie R. Collingsworth (Former COO Gates Foundation). This class gave me something infinitely greater than knowledge. Working with exceptional colleagues to help protect the United States from biological threats, both natural, accidental, and deliberate, was an extraordinary privilege that I am very grateful for. While I am proud of what we accomplished, working in government during this time was full of challenges, including the difficulty of interagency coordination and policymaking, the increasing complexity of defending against future biological threats, and an extraordinarily polarized, click-chasing media and political environment that degrades Americans' trust in government, in science, and in each other. Trust, it seems to me, is the special sauce that makes any complex social system, including government, work. But it isn't cheap, nor should it be. Towards the end of my time at DARPA, I had the chance to spend time thinking about how to build trusted and trustworthy systems to prevent a malicious actor (whether a terrorist or a rogue state) from using increasingly capable AI tools to build and deploy biological weapons, while also making sure that the vast majority of legitimate scientists can still use AI to unlock beneficial advances we haven't even dreamed of yet. This, it turns out, is a hard problem-but a motivating one! This past week, I had the pleasure of volunteering with Verdafield: Science in the Park during their rocketry‑themed program. As someone passionate about engineering outreach, I’m a big believer that college students should actively seek opportunities to mentor the next generation and develop their own leadership skills in the process. For my first time working with kids and rockets, I went in thinking my limited rocketry knowledge would be the bottleneck. Turns out, the real challenges came from the kids. A few takeaways from the week: • Meet kids where they are They don’t need a propulsion lecture; they need someone patient enough to show them how to cut a straight line and cheer when they get it right. For instance, some kids didn’t have prior experience with box cutters or even scissors, which we solved by having a safety demonstration and then correcting them based off that. • Instructions matter more than you think Our parachute-crafting activity had a lot of “creative freedoms” which is code for “chaos.” Kids thrive when the steps are clear and the diagrams look like the final product. • Elementary schools have recess for a reason Long lectures aren’t fun for kids and our first day was lecture-heavy which we realized halfway through. We ended up having lunch early that day, and for subsequent days, we had breaks every 60-80 minutes which worked out nicely. • Group work is rocket fuel Once we realized most kids couldn’t build a rocket solo, we switched to teams. My ROTC brain immediately went, “Ah yes, a Group Leadership Project,” and then started writing org charts based on which kids work well together. We also minimized interpersonal friction points by using OpenRocket to make the best rocket as opposed to opinions. On an amusing note, ROTC unintentionally makes great teachers. All that focus on people, structure, and mentorship translates surprisingly well to camp instruction. The culmination of that group work was a rocket that hit 500+ feet at 60 Acres (I let the kids record that video so pardon the language). There was also a bottle rocket with 67 fins. Yeah, six-seven. Can’t beat the magical numbers. Huge thanks to camp instructors Thomas Coffee and Shuonan Dong for letting me volunteer. I’m excited for next week’s bigger class which will be a doozy.

They finally said yes. We pitched. The crowd went wild. They moved us into the finals. And we won the entire competition unanimously. That moment felt like the last four years of building our company. We’ve constantly been dismissed, underestimated and overlooked. Some people see Drew and assume we’re a cute school project led by a disabled kid. They don’t see the full picture. Over half a million followers. More than 2 billion views. Millions in revenue. Hundreds of thousands of dollars donated to help people with disabilities. For years, I thought we needed the people at the top to believe in us. I was wrong. We needed the community to believe in us. They vote with their follows, their shares and their dollars. That’s the lesson. You don’t need everyone’s approval to build something meaningful. You need a purpose people can rally around, the courage to keep showing up and a community willing to fight beside you. That’s all people with disabilities are asking for. Not sympathy. Not special treatment. Just a fair shot. Because sometimes the people who almost never get the opportunity are the ones most capable of winning it all. Happy and excited to continue busting down doors for the disabled community for the rest of my life.

activity.title: Last week, I presented my first first-authored paper, accepted to Findings of #EACL 2026. This work started as my Bachelor’s thesis at the Indian Institute of Technology, Bombay , under Prof. Preethi Jyothi. I’ve been writing (and rewriting) this paper for nearly a year, through multiple rounds of reviews and rejections. Sometimes the feedback was absolutely right and pushed us to improve the work. Other times, the challenge was figuring out how to better communicate what we were trying to say. Interestingly, the final version of this paper came together after I moved to UC San Diego , where I gained a new perspective on research writing (and thinking). The process taught me two things I hope to carry with me: • If you keep showing up, things do eventually come together. • Sometimes, the best progress comes not from pushing harder, but from stepping back and returning with a fresh perspective. 💡 This work looks at a simple but very real problem: How do we identify languages when people switch between them mid-sentence? In our paper, “Improving Language Identification for Code-Switched Speech: The Pivotal Role of Accented English,” we study this problem in the context of code-switched speech. A key reason models struggle is accent mismatch: English sounds different depending on the matrix (dominant) language used in an utterance. By adapting models with small amounts of accent-matched English, we see strong improvements without hurting performance on standard monolingual speech. We also introduce LangRank, a ranking-based evaluation metric that better captures performance for language identification in code-switched utterances. 📄 Improving Language Identification for Code-Switched Speech: The Pivotal Role of Accented English https://lnkd.in/gmaDku8u Grateful for the mentorship, collaboration, and the journey this took. Here’s to many more drafts, dead ends, and hopefully, breakthroughs. ...more

Last week, I had the opportunity to attend Cornell, Maryland, Max Planck Pre-doctoral Research School in Computer Science (CMMRS) 2025, hosted at the Max Planck Institute for Software Systems (MPI-SWS) in Saarbrücken, Germany. Organized by three of the world’s leading research institutions — Max Planck Institute for Software Systems (MPI-SWS) , Cornell University , and the University of Maryland , the program brought together students and researchers from over 30 countries to explore foundational ideas in computer science. Across a week of lectures, panel discussions, and group mentoring sessions, we dived into not just technical ideas, but also big-picture questions: about graduate school, industry vs. academia, and what truly drives fulfillment in research careers. What I expected was a week of technical deep dives. What I didn’t expect was how much the conversations would stay with me. From formal sessions to late-night discussions with fellow attendees, the energy was contagious. We talked about research, career paths, and sometimes about the smallest cultural quirks: from how food is eaten in different countries to unexpected traditions globally. That kind of cross-cultural exchange wasn’t just refreshing, it was one of the most impactful takeaways of the entire week. But what I’ll remember most is the passion, the way professors smiled when they spoke about their work, the joy in explaining their choices, and the quiet conviction behind them. Some of them had left high-paying industry roles for academia, fully aware of what they were giving up, and yet, visibly fulfilled. It made me think: maybe the real question is not what to pursue, but why, and whether it brings you that same spark. After all, it is all about maximizing our happiness utility function! Grateful to Peter Druschel , Lorenzo Alvisi, and Adish Singla for organizing such an inspiring program. A heartfelt thanks to the professors who flew in or made time from their packed schedules to share their work and insights with us — your passion was truly contagious. And to everyone I met, thank you for the conversations, ideas, and memories that made this week unforgettable. 🫶 ...more

Thrilled to share our journey at Inter-IIT Tech Meet 13.0, where our project "FinSight" secured 1st place among 22 participating IITs! We developed a dynamic multi-agent Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system leveraging Pathway for real-time financial insights. We chose the financial domain as it involved many complex data structures in the form of tabular data combined with narrative data, making it complex for RAG systems. Additionally, this being a field of high industry demand made it a perfect problem to tackle. My key contributions in the project was in the design and execution of our Novel question decomposer architecture (Recursive Residual Resolution) from scratch. The key attribute of this architecture is that it dynamically creates and breaks down new questions based on the answered parts of the original question. Additionally, I also implemented 2 other key features - 1) Semantic caching, to store question-answer pairs and retrieve them the next time a similar question is asked. 2) Hosting our entire End to end RAG agent over a REST endpoint, using Pathway's serve callable functionality. I am grateful to have been given the opportunity to be a presenter alongside Adyasha Patra to a panel of Pathway's judges. After a rigorous round of evaluation over metrics such as code quality, technical proficiency, report submissions along with this final presentation, our team placed first among the total 22 IITs participating in this competition, while the Bombay contingent won Runner's up overall. At 16, I chose science over commerce because my handwriting was bad and IIT had objective exams. At 18, that logic somehow worked and I got into IIT. First engineer in a family of 16 people who have only ever run businesses. At 22, everyone around me was taking software roles. I did not take one. I had no plan, only a fairly strong feeling that I would end up building something of my own. At 24, I did. A legal SaaS company for US law firms. Part of it was a small voice agent that called hospitals to collect medical records, and it broke on us for months. At 25, I asked a few other founders how they tested their voice agents and found out none of them had a real answer either. So we shut down the legal company, started building the testing part properly, and got into Y Combinator with it. At 27, I moved to the US to scale Cekura . Today we test voice agents for teams running them at scale. We run them through thousands of calls before they go live, and once they are live we tell you which calls went badly so nobody has to sit and listen to all of them. Here is what I have learnt from all of it: If you had asked me at 22 what I would be doing at 27, I would not have said any of this. I would have described something much more sensible, and I would have been wrong about all of it. And if I sat down today and wrote out where I want to be at 32, I would probably be wrong about that too. I have stopped worrying about that. Most of what has worked out for me came from things I was not planning for, so I would rather keep building and find out.

The work is a core part of my master's thesis, developed with the CopeNLU group at the University of Copenhagen (Københavns Universitet). My poster session turned into a long run of sharp feedback and real conversations with people who care about steering and alignment as much as I do. The talks were just as good. Barbara Plank's keynote stole the show for me: her playful readings of the ACL logo and her case for keeping language at the heart of the field gave me a lot to sit with, especially with language tech moving as fast as it is right now. That session, plus sessions on cultural value alignment, low-resource NLP, and NLP for education, had me scribbling ideas nonstop. And the part that made the whole trip: finding the Vietnamese researchers at the conference. Swapping stories about our academic paths and wandering San Diego together made me feel at home, thousands of miles from Copenhagen. Seeing our community show up and lift each other on a stage like this made me really proud. None of it happens without the Danish Data Science Academy (DDSA), who funded my travel. activity.title: 🎓 This was my first summer running Early Career programs at Abridge , and stepping back into intern programming after a few years, I’m reminded of why I loooove this work. In my role I get a front-row seat to watch talented people find their footing and make an impact at a company that's moving fast in AI and healthcare. They worked on projects that are already shaping how care gets delivered: Enhancing our clinical decision support product, building a new demo of Abridge for Nurses, studying how conversations about exercise, sleep, and stress actually show up in primary care visits, and strengthening the safety systems that catch clinical errors before they ever reach a doctor. We held a fireside chat with our CTO San Oo and VP of Product Janie Lee yesterday, and something San said struck me. When asked about the amount of responsibility given to interns at Abridge, he said "You take any amount of responsibility that you want to take, and that's the limit. We built a Turing test that runs backwards. And watching people fail it was the best part. At the Tavus X Lovable hackathon this weekend, we flipped the premise: instead of an AI trying to convince you it's human, you have to convince an AI that you're a machine. You join a video call with a cold AI border agent guarding the "Machine World." To get in, you have to pass as an AI. It interrogates you for 60 seconds and it's brutal, because being human leaks out of you in ways you can't control: cadence, composure, diction and embodiment. Under the hood, the agent runs on Tavus - Phoenix-4 for the face, Raven for real-time perception. We wired custom tool calls so the instant it catches a tell, a structured event fires into our app, which holds the score and drives a live "Humanity Leak" meter. Try it out: https://lnkd.in/dAX9iG5w We flip the polarity here, it becomes a deepfake detector: you can catch AI pretending to be human. Synthetic candidates are already deepfaking their way through remote job interviews. Injected video is bypassing KYC checks in fintech and crypto onboarding. Shoutout to my teammate Alvin A. - none of this would've happened without him 🙌 . Also had a chat with Gagan Bhat from Anthropic on RL environments for AI agents and Claude.
